title: Where AI can aid chemistry research and where reliability falls short
excerpt: Researchers from the Skoltech AI Center, together with colleagues from the Zelinsky Institute of Organic Chemistry of the Russian Academy of Sciences, ITMO University and other institutions, have published a paper in Chemical Society Reviews that examines where AI produces measurable value in a chemical research workflow, how to assess its reliability and why a strong benchmark result does not necessarily translate into laboratory performance.
content_html:
Researchers from the Skoltech AI Center, together with colleagues from the Zelinsky Institute of Organic Chemistry of the Russian Academy of Sciences, ITMO University and other institutions, have published a paper in Chemical Society Reviews that examines where AI produces measurable value in a chemical research workflow, how to assess its reliability and why a strong benchmark result does not necessarily translate into laboratory performance.

Chemical research produces diverse information: scientific publications, images, spectra, measurements and reaction records. Understanding the relationship between molecular structure and properties remains essential. Researchers also make a sequence of practical decisions, including which evidence to examine, which experiment to run next and how to adjust the plan after a new result. The review uses this decision sequence as its organizing framework.

The authors divide chemical research into stages that generate, transform and validate information, and map AI methods onto each stage. They discuss classical machine learning, models that incorporate chemical knowledge and emerging foundation models for chemistry. Their emphasis is on measurable outcomes and recurring failure modes, rather than benchmark scores alone.

The review covers knowledge extraction from the scientific literature and accumulated data sets; interpretation of experimental data from spectroscopy, mass spectrometry and microscopy; prediction of properties and reactivity; synthesis planning; and systems in which the outcome of one experiment guides the next. Representative applications illustrate what can transfer to a new problem and where a method's limitations matter.

In their conclusion, the authors identify three ways AI can change a chemist's work. It can extract mechanistic insight from complex spectra, images and scientific texts; identify promising compounds, synthesis routes and experimental conditions from among many options; and connect predictions to automated experiments whose results guide the next step. The image above uses property prediction to show which steps between a molecular description and an experiment different models can perform. AI's practical value depends on whether it improves decisions under real research constraints.

"We wanted to look at AI from the perspective of a chemist who needs to make research decisions. A model's high accuracy on test data is only the tip of the iceberg. What matters more is whether it helps interpret measurements, plan informative experiments and maintain the quality and reliability of its predictions when working with new compounds and reactions," says Alexander Ryabov, senior research scientist at the Skoltech AI Center.

The authors examine risks that can inflate the apparent success of a model: information leakage between training and evaluation, overfitting to a limited set of examples and extrapolation errors beyond familiar data. These issues are especially consequential in chemistry, where substances, reaction conditions and instruments vary, while experimental validation takes time and resources. Before using a model, the authors advise checking whether its training data match the compounds and instruments of a particular laboratory, how reliably it estimates prediction uncertainty and whether it has been tested on new experiments whose results were not known during training.

"The next stage of AI in chemistry will bring together advanced large language models (LLMs) and physics-informed models that respect chemical constraints. An AI agent must assess when a physics-informed model's prediction is well founded, when it goes beyond the data used to train it and which experiment would best reduce uncertainty. The researcher, in turn, remains responsible for defining the scientific question and verifying the results produced by the AI agent," says Michael G. Medvedev, head of the Theoretical Chemistry Group at the Zelinsky Institute of Organic Chemistry and first author of the review.
